name: Opposition to immigration
summary: Opposition to immigration holds that a country should sharply reduce or stop immigration, on grounds of cultural continuity, national sovereignty over borders, fiscal and labor-market burden, and security. Adherents typically want immigrants who remain to assimilate, welfare reserved for citizens, and stricter citizenship. The position cuts across the economic left and right, and its strands range from civic to ethnic nationalism.
scope: The mainstream of contemporary restrictionism as expressed by populist and national-conservative parties (Sweden Democrats, One Nation, Hungary's government) and the historical Powell speech of 1968. It excludes ethnonationalist and white-supremacist fringes (remigration, race-mixing bans), and since the ideology has no economic program, most non-immigration answers are low-confidence inferences.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Restrictionist parties are split: Sweden Democrats back a welfare state but for citizens, while US and Australian strands are market-leaning; the ideology itself has no line on health systems.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Some restrictionists argue immigration undercuts low wages and favor wage floors, others are market-leaning; the position is not defined by the ideology.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Adherents range from free-market conservatives to welfare-state nationalists, so the ideology is indifferent on markets in general.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Nationalist-populist parties are divided between tax-cutting and populist redistribution; the opposition to immigration is independent of this.

unions-good.rationale: Restrictionists sometimes cite worker wage protection, yet many parties are indifferent or hostile to unions; no settled stance.

property-fundamental.rationale: No documented position; adherents vary between property-rights conservatives and welfare nationalists.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Hanson attacks elites and bureaucrats but not corporate regulation as such; the ideology is split on it.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Sweden Democrats support the welfare state but limit it to citizens and residents, so the claim that welfare as such should be cut is not the ideology's, while others in the family do favor cuts.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Restrictionists typically complain that criticism of immigration is silenced and reject laws on hate speech as curbs on open debate; Powell similarly argued against anti-discrimination law.

strong-leader.rationale: Populist rhetoric against elites can favor decisive leaders, but many restrictionist parties operate within parliaments and defend constitutional order.

limit-guns.rationale: No documented position; restrictionists in the US and Australia lean pro-gun, though European strands are mixed.

empower-police-military.rationale: Border enforcement, deportation and crime-and-security arguments lead restrictionists to favor stronger police and border forces.

decide-locally.rationale: Some propose devolution to local communities, but restrictionists mostly want national control over borders; split.

traditional-family.rationale: Social-conservative stance common among national-conservative parties, but not definitional to opposing immigration.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Adherents are split: some Western populist parties accept it or use it against Islam, while others oppose it.

abortion-legal.rationale: No shared position among restrictionist parties, which vary from pro-choice to pro-life.

more-religion-public.rationale: Some stress a Christian cultural heritage, others are secular and oppose Islam on secular grounds; split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Hanson ended with 'one people, one nation' and attacked the 'Aboriginal industry' and special group programs; Powell objected to a 'privileged or special class', so adherents reject group-targeted remedies.

gender-social-construct.rationale: National-conservative strands tend to reject it, though not part of the core.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Cultural preservation is one of the central stated reasons for restricting immigration, and a shared national and cultural identity is a stated aim of the Sweden Democrats.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Reducing immigration is the defining position: Hanson wanted it halted short term, Powell wanted inflow cut to 'negligible proportions', and Sweden Democrats seek asylum migration near zero.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: In her maiden speech Hanson called for UN treaties to be exposed and repudiated as threats to Australian control, and the Sweden Democrats oppose shifting power to the EU.

free-trade.rationale: Adherents are divided between market-liberal restrictionists and protectionist populists; Hanson was protectionist, other parties are not.

nation-first.rationale: Restrictionism puts the national interest and the right to decide admissions ahead of cosmopolitan duties; SEP lists national interest and self-determination among its arguments.

open-borders.rationale: Open borders are the direct opposite of the ideology; SEP treats restriction as the opposing pole.

limit-growth.rationale: Some restrictionists use environmental strain and population growth as an argument against immigration, but they do not generally call for limits on economic growth.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Mixed: some Greens-adjacent restrictionists cite sustainability, but most national-populist parties are skeptical of drastic climate policy.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mainstream restrictionist parties work through elections; the rare militant strand differs.

experts-over-public.rationale: Populist restrictionists present themselves as against out-of-touch elites and bureaucrats and favor popular opinion on immigration.

basic-income.rationale: Restrictionists generally prefer welfare linked to citizenship and work, which is hard to square with an unconditional income.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Hanson-style populists favor protection, while market-liberal restrictionists do not; split.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Some populist parties attack central banks, others do not.

one-party-rule.rationale: Restrictionist parties compete in multiparty elections; Hanson attacks the big parties but wants more representation, not one-party rule.

democracy-best.rationale: Populist restrictionists commonly appeal to the will of the voters, citing majorities who want less immigration, though they dispute elite-driven outcomes.

direct-votes.rationale: Referendums are used by restrictionists (for instance Hungary's 2016 quota vote), though not universal.

natural-rulers.rationale: Populists say they oppose elites, but the ideology does not generally endorse natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: Mainstream restrictionist parties disavow violence, but not a stated principle.

war-builds-character.rationale: Not part of the mainstream restrictionist program.

separate-church-state.rationale: Split between secular and Christian-heritage strands.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Control of borders and security is a core state function in restrictionist arguments.

military-superiority.rationale: Restrictionist parties differ on defense spending and the sources give no common line on military superiority over rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The strands split: ethnic-nationalists want a mono-ethnic nation, civic restrictionists like the Sweden Democrats say foreign-born people can become Swedish by assimilating.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Hanson called for sweeping changes to Aboriginal affairs and attacked separate Aboriginal programs.

civilizational-union.rationale: Some restrictionists favour defending a Western or European civilization, others stress sovereign nations; split.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Sweden Democrats' citizenship proposals stress loyalty and duties, but this is not a general stance.

limit-population.rationale: Some cite population growth and sprawl in the case for restriction, but they do not call for limiting native births.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Restrictionists cite research and results when arguing their case, but also appeal to identity and principle; no consistent stance.

direct-action.rationale: Mainstream restrictionism works through parties and elections.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Welfare for citizens only, conditional on membership, runs against universal need-based distribution.

taxation-theft.rationale: Sweden Democrats support a welfare state; some in the family differ.

conscription.rationale: Nationalist parties differ on national service, and Hanson called for it while others do not, so this is split.

media-academia-power.rationale: Restrictionists commonly claim that media and academia suppress debate on immigration, and Hanson attacked bureaucrats and 'do-gooders'.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Present in some ethnonationalist strands, rejected by civic restrictionists; the article ties opposition more to ethnocentrism.

national-rebirth.rationale: Some strands speak of national renewal, others do not.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Restrictionism focuses on closing borders, not expanding them.

universal-morality.rationale: Restrictionists dispute that universal duties require open admission, but they do not generally deny universal morals; no clear stance.

single-common-good.rationale: Appeals to one national identity point one way while parties compete as interest-based; no documented line.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Views differ: some European restrictionists are pro-Israel, others hostile.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language of the state matters in citizenship tests, but reviving a lapsed language is not a restrictionist concern.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education funding models are not part of the immigration debate and parties differ.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal burden of immigrants is argued, yet adherents split on general deficit policy.

economic-freedom.rationale: Market-liberal and welfare-nationalist strands disagree about the link between political and economic freedom.

national-self-determination.rationale: Restrictionists justify border control by their own nation's right to self-government, as in the Sweden Democrats' sovereignty campaigns; the sources do not speak of every nation.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The Sweden Democrats oppose welfare for people who are not citizens or permanent residents, and welfare burden is a core restrictionist argument.

class-collaboration.rationale: Hanson blamed elites yet stressed national unity, and parties vary on the employer-worker relation.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Defense of inherited national culture and tradition is central, so sacrificing heritage institutions is rejected.

workers-nation.rationale: Restrictionists frame workers as a national group needing protection from low-wage competition, but this is partial.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Social-conservative parties lean toward it, while others in the family are liberal on gender; split.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Mainstream restrictionism rejects legally enforced racial separation and the Sweden Democrats say the foreign-born can become Swedish; ethnonationalist fringes dissent.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy policy differs across restrictionist parties and is not tied to immigration.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Hanson demanded immigrants' "full, undivided loyalty" and attacked ethnic ghettos, and the Sweden Democrats prefer assimilation to multicultural integration; neither says immigrants must give up their original culture.

elite-replacement.rationale: The Great Replacement idea is held by part of the far right, but mainstream restrictionists mostly cite elite indifference, not deliberate replacement; adherents are split.

proportional-representation.rationale: Parties benefit differently under each system.

national-mission.rationale: Nation-first restrictionists generally do not seek to spread their government abroad.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Hanson attacked 'fat cats, bureaucrats and do-gooders' and populism is tied to anti-immigration attitudes in the article.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Border control is a core state function, but adherents differ on a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Present on the ethnonationalist fringe but not in mainstream restrictionism.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Mainstream restrictionists formally accept equal worth and legal equality for citizens but deny equal claims to admission, so the answer is mixed.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist internal debate with no bearing on restrictionist doctrine.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The article notes that framing immigrants as colonizers comes from decolonization advocates; restrictionist nationalists reject describing their own states that way.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Restrictionists do not seek laws on conversion; a concern about Islam does not translate to restricting individual conversion.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Christian-heritage and secular strands disagree on religious instruction in schools.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A socialist-state doctrine; restrictionists reject socialism, so they would not endorse a stronger socialist state.

trade-surplus.rationale: Protectionist strands favor it, liberals do not.

population-transfer.rationale: Powell backed voluntary re-emigration with grants and some activists promote remigration, but most restrictionist parties do not call for forcing anyone out, so adherents are split.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The state's authority to enforce borders and deport conflicts with an absolute rule.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social-Darwinist strands exist on the fringe, but mainstream restrictionism does not state this.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Adherents often protest bans of their own parties, though not uniformly.

separated-powers.rationale: Support for constitutional order is typical, but populists attack judges blocking deportations; mixed.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Welfare for citizens first is an inverse of this, but poor-first language appears in the populist stance; split.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Labor law is not part of the restrictionist program, and populist parties differ on unions.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Some cite population pressure abroad, but adherents generally do not stress it.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Opponents argue that immigrants form separate communities, the Sweden Democrats say a shared identity underlies cohesion, and Hanson said a multicultural country 'can never be strong or united'.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Security arguments push partly toward yes, but adherents differ.

party-controls-media.rationale: Restrictionists claim that existing media silence them, so they resist control of media by a ruling party.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The Sweden Democrats seek strict citizenship requirements including language, cultural knowledge and loyalty, and SEP notes delayed benefits as a middle path.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The Sweden Democrats oppose power shifting to the EU, and Hungary rejected EU migrant quotas.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Constitutional design differs across the countries where restrictionist parties operate.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Hanson-style isolationism favors it, but other parties support alliances like NATO; split.

people-in-arms.rationale: Gun-rights supporters among restrictionists might like it, but the sources contain no stated position.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Education is the strongest predictor of opposition in the article, and populist adherents attack 'do-gooders' and elites as out of touch.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Opposition to multiculturalism rests on the claim that cultures differ in ways that matter, but some adherents call cultures merely different, so the answer leans disagree with dissent.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Social conservatives within the family oppose it, but no stated position.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Restrictionists tend to favour descent or strict naturalisation over birthright citizenship, and the Sweden Democrats want citizenship earned, but the sources state no rule.

minority-language-support.rationale: Hanson wanted one people, and assimilation is demanded; support for minority-language provision runs counter.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Opposition to separate customs and parallel communities makes exemptions from general laws unwelcome.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The article notes some restrictionists favor aid in origin countries instead of admitting migrants, but Hanson opposed foreign aid; a duty to give substantial aid is not accepted.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Defense posture differs between restrictionist parties and is not tied to immigration.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Populists attack central banks in some places and accept them in others; split.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Market-liberal and welfare-nationalist strands differ on the limits of property.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Strands differ: secular ones want religion subordinate to the state in relation to Islam, while Christian-heritage ones do not.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Constitutional preferences vary by country, and nothing is stated.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure is not a restrictionist issue, and market-liberal and welfare-nationalist strands differ.

character-from-environment.rationale: Environmental and innate views are both found.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Not part of the ideology; parties compete under constitutions.

space-expansion.rationale: No restrictionist source addresses space policy.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Restrictionists demand assimilation and an end to multiculturalism rather than separate minority institutions.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Split: economic-nationalist strands favour protection but market-liberal strands favour trade.

public-money-creation.rationale: The ideology has no monetary program and adherents range from market-leaning to populist.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Powell opposed race-relations law, but civic-nationalist strands accept anti-discrimination law; adherents are split.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: No documented position on resistance to rulers; populist strands appeal to people against elites but that is not defined by the ideology.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Not defined by the ideology; welfare-chauvinist strands support the needy at home but others oppose redistribution.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The ideology concerns migration not territory; Hungary's government has made some such claims, but the strand is split.

paid-care-work.rationale: No documented position; strands are split.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Restrictionists are split between socially conservative and liberal strands on divorce.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Populists favour direct democracy in places, but the ideology has no position on binding delegates.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Restrictionists are split between market-leaning and welfare-state strands on pensions.

single-official-language.rationale: Assimilation is a core restrictionist demand, and a common national language is its usual first requirement.

residents-only-property.rationale: The ideology is about who enters the country, not who may buy property, and adherents are split on local purchase limits.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employment policy is outside the ideology and its parties split between market-leaning and welfare-state positions.

democratic-peace.rationale: The ideology takes no line on democracy promotion; adherents are often sceptical of foreign adventures but others back a democratic West.

non-intervention.rationale: Restrictionists tend to favour staying out of foreign conflicts but many back intervention against security threats, so no common line.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure is unrelated to the ideology and adherents span left and right economic positions.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The mainstream strand in scope rejects the Great Replacement-style conspiracy claims that belong to the ethnonationalist fringe the profile excludes.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Adherents are split: populists attack secretive elites, while national-security arguments favour confidentiality.

informal-organisation.rationale: These adherents mostly organise through parties such as the Sweden Democrats and One Nation, not informal affinity groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Control of borders is argued as a sovereign right, so adherents want national law to prevail over international courts and refugee rules.

religious-nation.rationale: Strands range from civic to ethnic nationalism, and the Sweden Democrats and One Nation define belonging by culture more than faith, while Hungary's government stresses Christian identity.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The ideology has no regional fiscal line and adherents are split, so this is left neutral.

defeat-communism.rationale: Anti-communism is not part of the stance itself, and some adherents hold it while others do not.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Restrictionist parties are split between welfare-state and market-leaning positions, with no line on who delivers services.

religion-illusion.rationale: The stance concerns immigration, and adherents are split between religious defenders of cultural heritage and secular ones.

treaties-binding.rationale: The ideology has no line on treaties with internal nations; adherents are split.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The ideology has no economic programme and strands accept either capitalism or welfare arrangements.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Restrictionists stress a nation's ancestral ties and cultural continuity, though the civic strand rests on citizenship rather than descent.

holocaust-denial.rationale: No cited source discusses Holocaust denial; rejection is assumed because the scope covers mainstream parties and excludes ethnonationalist fringes.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Restrictionist parties compete in elections and complain of being shut out, so they oppose suppression of opposition.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Populist parties favour referendums and distrust distant officials, though they do not stress workplace or university participation.

assisted-dying.rationale: Adherents are split and the ideology has no position.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Restrictionist populists often claim to be beyond left and right, as the Sweden Democrats do with welfare-plus-nationalism.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Many restrictionist parties argue that Islam clashes with national culture, but civic strands dispute this, so adherents are split.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The movement stresses border security and sovereignty, which presuppose armed forces.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Adherents differ, from Atlanticist to sovereigntist; no common position.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Restrictionism has no economic programme; adherents are split on mutual banking.

property-franchise.rationale: Restrictionist parties are electoral and populist and defend universal suffrage for citizens; a property bar is not part of the platform.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Populist restrictionists often attack media elites as hostile, but they do not generally attack property in presses; adherents are split.

online-participation.rationale: The ideology has no line on online participation; populist parties often favour referendums but adherents are split on internet deliberation.

open-government-data.rationale: Anti-elite populists may favour transparency, but the ideology has no stated line on open records; adherents are split.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The mainstream scope rejects race and religion tests for the vote, but some adherents back cultural criteria for entry; most would not support marriage law restrictions.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Restrictionist parties are split between market-leaning and welfare-protecting economics, and the ideology has no economic line.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: The ideology has no line on this; adherents are split between socially conservative and liberal-nationalist strands (some Western parties are gay-friendly).

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Restrictionists emphasise preserving national cultural and religious heritage, and the position is hostile to state secularist imposition; the Sweden Democrats and Hungary's government defend Christian heritage.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Security and law and order, including deporting criminal immigrants, are core arguments for restriction, so abolition is firmly opposed.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Adherents are split: welfare-state nationalists want benefits reserved for citizens, while market-leaning strands favour private help.

term-limits.rationale: The ideology takes no position on terms in office and adherents across populist parties are split.

rent-control.rationale: The ideology has no housing policy and restrictionist parties split between market-leaning and welfare-protective positions.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Restrictionism has no settled line on genocide recognition; individual parties differ by their own national history.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The ideology has no economic programme and its adherents range from market-liberal to welfare-chauvinist.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Adherents differ; some national-conservative movements honour fallen soldiers while civic strands do not use saint language.

culture-before-state.rationale: Cultural continuity is central to the case, but the ideology has no stand on the order of cultural and state projects.

god-not-male.rationale: The ideology is indifferent to theological language for God, and its adherents split between religious conservatives and secular voters.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The mainstream scope excludes ethnonationalist fringes; civic restrictionists want assimilation of immigrants, not control of the economy by ethnic groups, while others lean the other way.

independent-unions.rationale: The ideology has no labour programme; restrictionist parties are split on unions.

person-over-state.rationale: Restrictionists emphasize the national community but do not usually deny individual worth; adherents are split.

dense-cities.rationale: Adherents are split; some blame dense, immigrant-heavy cities, others do not address the question.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The mainstream strand covered by the scope rests on civic or cultural arguments and rejects racial organizing, which belongs to excluded fringes.

free-public-college.rationale: The ideology has no education-funding line, and restrictionist parties range from welfare-state to market-leaning.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Nothing in the restrictionist case concerns gendered values, and adherents are split.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Populist adherents distrust elite deals, but the ideology has no stated position on diplomatic secrecy.

capital-controls.rationale: Restrictionists are split between market-leaning and economic-nationalist strands, so no common line on capital movement.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The ideology has no line on arms monopoly; restrictionist parties differ, with gun rights stronger in the US than in Europe.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Parties are split between pro-union welfare nationalists and market-leaning ones; no ideology-level line.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Sweden Democrats back welfare for citizens while market-leaning strands do not, so the ideology has no line.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Restrictionism has no economic programme and its parties differ on fiscal policy.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The ideology has no economic blueprint; adherents are split.

sacred-nation.rationale: Cultural continuity is a central argument for restriction, and the nationalist strand treats the nation as an enduring community, but civic and economic strands do not hold it sacred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Strands range from civic to ethnic nationalists, and ethnonationalist strands deny universal rights while others affirm them, so adherents are split.

public-service-media.rationale: Adherents split between wanting public broadcasters kept and attacking them as elite and biased; no ideology-level line.

ban-fgm.rationale: Restrictionist parties cite FGM and honour practices brought by immigrants as reasons for restriction and back bans, and the Sweden Democrats support strict enforcement.

one-language-many-names.rationale: The statement is about regional naming of languages, which restrictionism does not address; adherents split between unified and regional views.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: The ideology has no environmental programme and its parties differ from market-liberal to interventionist; no stance is documented.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Restrictionist parties are split between environmental nationalism, as in Sweden Democrats' local conservation, and climate scepticism; no shared line exists.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Restrictionist parties campaign on law and order and tougher penalties, but no cited source calls for sentences fixed by law.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Assimilation is a core demand: the summary and the Sweden Democrats' programme require immigrants to learn the national language and to adopt national culture.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: The position has no economic programme and adherents range from left to right, so this is genuinely split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Adherents are split between defending a Christian national heritage and opposing special accommodation for any religion; no stated common line.

women-suffrage.rationale: Not contested in the mainstream strand sampled; Hanson and the Sweden Democrats operate within universal suffrage.

race-social-construct.rationale: The mainstream strand frames its case as cultural, not racial, yet the ethnonationalist fringe asserts race; adherents are split.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Restrictionists defend a cultural and often Christian heritage but are not united on literal scripture; the issue is outside the movement's concerns.

equal-conscription.rationale: The movement has no common position on conscription of women; national-conservative adherents are split.

self-ownership.rationale: The ideology has no position on self-ownership; liberal and communitarian restrictionists split.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Consumption taxes are not part of restrictionism, and adherents differ by party.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Restrictionists want welfare reserved for citizens (s4), but not specifically targeted at the poor; adherents are split.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Populist adherents attack elites but operate through parties, so the sources give no clear line.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: The ideology has no financial policy; populist-right parties are generally sceptical of new international taxes and global institutions, an inference from their sovereignty stance.

automate-paid-work.rationale: The ideology has no automation line; some strands cite automation against importing labour, others value work, so adherents are split.

police-more-powers.rationale: Border enforcement, deportation and crime-and-security arguments lead restrictionists to favor stronger police and border forces. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

missingStatements.text: A country should be able to deport immigrants who commit serious crimes.
missingStatements.rationale: Deportation and returns are central restrictionist policy alongside border enforcement, and are cited in the article's policy list.

missingStatements.text: Asylum seekers should be turned back or processed outside the country rather than admitted to claim asylum on its territory.
missingStatements.rationale: The Sweden Democrats seek asylum migration near zero and the article lists deterrence and returns as policy.

missingStatements.text: Immigration costs the receiving country more in public spending than immigrants contribute.
missingStatements.rationale: The fiscal-burden claim is a main economic argument, while research cited in the article is contested.
missingStatements.declined: Fiscal-cost claim is an empirical, contested one that reduce-immigration and welfare-for-citizens already place; not worth a bank slot.

missingStatements.text: Governments should be able to decide whom to admit as a matter of national self-determination.
missingStatements.rationale: SEP treats political self-determination as a leading argument for restriction, and restrictionist parties frame admission as a sovereign choice.

notes: Strands differ: civic-assimilationist (Sweden Democrats), economic-protectionist (Hanson on unemployment), and ethnonationalist (replacement theory, remigration). Non-immigration answers vary by country; most are therefore low confidence.
